summary.title: Low density interior in supercooled aqueous nanodroplets expels ions to the subsurface
summary.authors: Shahrazad M A Malek, Ivan Saika-Voivod, Styliani Consta
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the spatial distribution of sodium ions in supercooled aqueous nanodroplets using molecular dynamics simulations and an analytical reference model. The authors demonstrate that at room temperature, the radial distribution of a single Na+ ion is nearly uniform within the droplet core, consistent with a newly proposed "electrostatic confinement" model that predicts a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass. However, at supercooled temperatures (200 K), the internal structure of the water changes significantly. A low-density core with tetrahedral ordering forms, surrounded by a high-density, more disordered subsurface. The simulations reveal that Na+ ions are expelled from this low-density tetrahedral core and preferentially reside in the denser subsurface region. This behavior contrasts with room temperature conditions and cannot be explained by the standard non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation, which assumes a homogeneous dielectric. The study highlights the critical role of solvent structure in determining ion location, with implications for atmospheric aerosols and mass spectrometry techniques like electrospray ionization. The findings suggest that the heterogeneous environment of supercooled droplets fundamentally alters ion solvation, potentially affecting chemical reactivity and the preservation of macromolecular conformations. The authors propose that this work serves as a starting point for understanding the structure of supercooled electrosprayed droplets used in native mass spectrometry.

claims.description: Supercooled aqueous nanodroplets expel ions to the subsurface due to a low-density tetrahedral core.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the spatial distribution of sodium ions in supercooled aqueous nanodroplets using molecular dynamics simulations and an analytical reference model. The authors demonstrate that at room temperature, the radial distribution of a single Na+ ion is nearly uniform within the droplet core, consistent with a newly proposed "electrostatic confinement" model that predicts a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass. However, at supercooled temperatures (200 K), the internal structure of the water changes significantly. A low-density core with tetrahedral ordering forms, surrounded by a high-density, more disordered subsurface. The simulations reveal that Na+ ions are expelled from this low-density tetrahedral core and preferentially reside in the denser subsurface region. This behavior contrasts with room temperature conditions and cannot be explained by the standard non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation, which assumes a homogeneous dielectric. The study highlights the critical role of solvent structure in determining ion location, with implications for atmospheric aerosols and mass spectrometry techniques like electrospray ionization. The findings suggest that the heterogeneous environment of supercooled droplets fundamentally alters ion solvation, potentially affecting chemical reactivity and the preservation of macromolecular conformations. The authors propose that this work serves as a starting point for understanding the structure of supercooled electrosprayed droplets used in native mass spectrometry.

Research Context
The spatial distribution of ions in droplets is crucial for chemical reactivity in aerosols. Previous studies focused on room temperature or small clusters up to 100 water molecules. Supercooled clusters are challenging to equilibrate, limiting prior computational studies. Recent simulations revealed an anomalous inverted radial density profile in supercooled water. A low-density core with tetrahedral ordering was observed in larger supercooled droplets. The distribution of ions in supercooled droplets remains completely unknown.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study investigates the location of single and multiple ions in supercooled aqueous clusters. The authors hypothesize that the low-density core differentiates ion distribution from room temperature. They propose that ions will be expelled from the tetrahedral core to the subsurface. An analytical model is introduced to explain forces determining ion location. The model predicts a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass. This effect is named "electrostatic confinement" (EC).

Methodological Details
Simulations were performed using GROMACS v4.6.1 molecular dynamics. Water was modeled with the TIP4P/2005 potential. Na+ ions used OPLS-AA parameters with a charge of +1e. Temperatures studied were 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K. System sizes ranged from 100 to 1100 water molecules. Simulations were run in the canonical ensemble with Nosé-Hoover thermostat. Equilibration was verified by comparing runs starting from center and surface. Voronoi volumes and tetrahedral order parameters were calculated for structure analysis.

Procedures And Architectures
The analytical model sums electrostatic and surface energy of a deformable droplet. The energy related to ion distance from COM is harmonic. The spring constant K(ε) depends on the dielectric constant. Maximum confinement occurs at ε ≈ 2.73. Simulations used a leap-frog algorithm with a 2 fs time step. Cutoff for interactions was set to L/2 to capture long-range effects. Relaxation times were estimated from neighbor correlation functions.

Key Results
At 300 K, the Na+ radial distribution is nearly uniform in the core. At 200 K, the Na+ peak shifts to the subsurface region. The subsurface peak coincides with the peak in Voronoi-based density. Multiple ions also show a maximum at the subsurface location at 200 K. The tetrahedral order parameter decreases at the subsurface density peak. The distance to the fifth neighbor increases at the subsurface, indicating disorder. For 776 H2O at 300 K, ion decay fits an exponential with λPB ≈ 1.2 nm. For 1100 H2O at 300 K, ion decay fits an exponential with λPB ≈ 1.3 nm.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Ions prefer the high-density, disordered subsurface over the low-density tetrahedral core. The dielectric constant increases with density, favoring subsurface residence. The electrostatic confinement model explains room temperature behavior but not supercooling. The heterogeneous solvent structure at supercooling drives ion expulsion from the core. This finding challenges standard Poisson-Boltzmann predictions for supercooled droplets.

Contradictions And Limitations
The electrostatic confinement model fails to predict ion location at supercooling. Small clusters (N=100) do not form a tetrahedral core due to shape fluctuations. Sampling is challenging, requiring simulation times of 10-100 ns. The model does not account for ion size or hydrophobic effects. Evaporative cooling effects are not fully captured in the simulations.

Claims
Supercooled aqueous nanodroplets expel ions to the subsurface due to a low-density tetrahedral core. The Na+ peak is located within 0.1 nm of the subsurface density peak. The tetrahedral order parameter decreases at the subsurface. At room temperature, the ion distribution is nearly uniform. This affects chemical reactivity in atmospheric aerosols. It impacts the interpretation of mass spectrometry data.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Equilibration was tested by starting ions at the center and surface. Results were consistent across different starting conditions.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 plots the spring constant K(ε) versus dielectric constant. Figure 3 shows radial density profiles for pure water and Na+ ions. Figure 4 details the structure and ion location for N=776 at 200 K and 300 K. Figure 5 compares multiple ion distributions at 300 K and 200 K.

Three Takeaways
1. Supercooled droplets have a low-density tetrahedral core that expels ions to the subsurface. 2. The electrostatic confinement model explains room temperature ion distribution but not supercooling. 3. This work provides a starting point for studying supercooled electrosprayed droplets.
